title: Teach Us to Pray; Signs, Light, and Woes
summary: Jesus teaches his disciples the Lord's Prayer and encourages bold, persistent asking of a Father who gives the Holy Spirit. Accused of driving out demons by Beelzebul, he answers that he does so by the finger of God and that the kingdom has come. He warns a generation seeking signs that only the sign of Jonah will be given, speaks of the eye as the body's lamp, and at a Pharisee's table pronounces woes on Pharisees and experts in the law.
story: Jesus is on the road to Jerusalem, teaching as he goes. After Mary sat at his feet to listen in chapter 10, this chapter begins with the disciples asking him to teach them to pray, and prayer runs through its first thirteen verses. The rest of the chapter turns to conflict. The charge that Jesus works by Satan's power and the demand for a sign show that his opponents are hardening, and the meal with a Pharisee ends in a sharp exchange that leaves the scribes and Pharisees plotting to trap him. The chapter shows the two responses to Jesus side by side: humble asking and suspicious testing.
historical:
Luke's version of the Lord's Prayer is shorter than Matthew's (Matthew 6:9-13), which adds Our, in heaven, your will be done, and deliver us from the evil one. The two forms may come from different occasions, since Jesus probably taught the prayer more than once, or from different traditions of the same teaching preserved in different churches. The closing words of praise familiar in many churches (For yours is the kingdom) are not in the earliest manuscripts of either Gospel; they appear in an early Christian manual, the Didache, and entered later manuscripts from church use. John the Baptist had evidently taught his followers a distinctive prayer, as other Jewish teachers did.

Beelzebul is a form of Baal-zebub, the name of the god of the Philistine city of Ekron in 2 Kings 1, which Jews used as a name for the prince of demons. Exorcism was practiced by other Jewish healers of the time, which gives force to Jesus' question about their sons (verse 19). The Pharisees are described in the note on chapter 5.
cultural:
The friend at midnight depends on village life: bread was baked in the morning for the day, a guest had to be fed, and hospitality was a matter of the whole village's honor. A peasant family often slept together on a mat in a single room, so getting up and unbarring the door would wake everyone. The Greek word in verse 8 usually translated persistence means shamelessness, and interpreters debate whose shamelessness is meant: the boldness of the one who asks, or the sleeper's wish to avoid the shame of refusing hospitality. Either way, the lesson is the contrast with God: if a sleepy neighbor gives, how much more the Father.

Washing hands before a meal was a Pharisaic purity custom (Mark 7:3-4), not a command of the Law for ordinary Israelites. The Law required a tithe of produce; Pharisees extended it to small garden herbs such as mint and rue. Touching a grave made a person unclean (Numbers 19:16), so unmarked graves were a hidden hazard. Zechariah, killed in the temple court (2 Chronicles 24:20-22), is the last murder recorded in Chronicles, the final book in the traditional order of the Hebrew Bible, so from Abel to Zechariah spans the whole of Scripture.
literary: The prayer section moves from a model prayer (1-4) to a parable (5-8) to sayings (9-10) to a comparison from lesser to greater (11-13). Luke ends with the Father giving the Holy Spirit where Matthew 7:11 has good things, in keeping with his emphasis on the Spirit. The controversy section is built from sayings joined by theme: a divided kingdom, the stronger man, the returning spirit, true blessedness, the sign of Jonah, and the lamp. The meal ends with six woes in two sets of three, first against Pharisees (42-44), then against experts in the law (46-52), a pattern that recalls the woes of the prophets. Much of this chapter has parallels scattered through Matthew 6, 7, 12, and 23.

outline.t: The friend at midnight; ask, seek, knock
The returning spirit and true blessedness
Woes to the experts in the law

doctrines.note: Jesus teaches disciples to call God Father, to put his name and kingdom first, and then to ask for bread, forgiveness, and protection. Prayer is bold because the one who hears it is a good Father who gives his own Spirit.
Driving out demons by the finger of God shows that the kingdom has come upon Jesus' hearers. A stronger one has overpowered the strong man and is taking back what he held.

Jesus insists that God made the inside as well as the outside. Holiness is not external cleanliness while the heart is full of greed, but justice and the love of God, without neglecting lesser duties.

words.note: Epiousios, usually translated daily. The word is extremely rare outside this prayer, and its meaning has been debated since the early church: bread for today, bread for the coming day, or bread needed for existence. Each suggests humble dependence on God one day at a time.

Anaideia, shamelessness. This is its only New Testament use. It usually carries a negative sense, the lack of a proper sense of shame. Its application in the parable, to the asker or to the neighbor, is debated, as the cultural note explains.

Semeion, sign. In John a sign is something that reveals Jesus' identity. Here the crowd demands proof on their terms. Jesus refuses, offering only the sign of Jonah: his preaching that calls for repentance, and, as Matthew makes explicit, his coming out of death.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus as the one who knows the Father and teaches others to call him Father too. It shows him as the stronger one who defeats Satan, acting by the finger of God, a phrase from Exodus 8:19, where Pharaoh's magicians admit that God himself is at work in the plagues. Twice he says that one greater is here: greater than Solomon, whose wisdom drew the Queen of the South from the ends of the earth, and greater than Jonah, whose preaching brought Nineveh to repentance. Jesus claims to be the fulfillment of Israel's wisdom and prophecy, and to stand at the center of the judgment on this generation. His last words to the lawyers, about the blood of the prophets, foreshadow his own death at the hands of the same leaders.

hard.q: Are Jesus' woes fair to the Pharisees, and have they been used against Jewish people?
hard.a:
The difficulty is real on both counts. The Pharisees were not all hypocrites; many were devout people seeking to honor God in daily life, and some in Luke invite Jesus to dinner, warn him of danger (13:31), and later become believers (Acts 15:5). Paul was proud of having been a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5). Jesus' woes are prophetic speech in the tradition of Isaiah and Amos, spoken inside Israel by a Jew to fellow Jews, aimed at particular failures: outward religion without mercy, burdens laid on others, and resistance to God's messengers. Such warnings address every religious person, and the church has its own long record of the same sins.

It is also true that Christians have at times read passages like this as condemnations of Jews as a people, and that this reading contributed to contempt and violence against Jewish communities over centuries. Most Christian interpreters today reject it as a misuse of the text. Read in context, Jesus' woes call religious leaders, including the reader's own, to justice and the love of God.

questions: The Lord's Prayer begins with God's name and kingdom before our needs. How does praying in that order change what you ask for?
Jesus says the Father will give the Holy Spirit to those who ask. What would you ask God for if you believed he was as good as Jesus says?
Which of Jesus' woes, if spoken to your church or to you, would land hardest, and why?
